title: Who Repairs the Internet in Wartime?
gist: Argues the U.S. lacks any wartime strategy to repair submarine cables if adversaries cut several in multiple theaters faster than the ~22-ship global repair fleet can restore them, citing Russian Svalbard rehearsals, Chinese-owned Pacific repair capacity, insurance withdrawal and legal targeting risk. Proposes critical-infrastructure designation, a federal coordinator, an expanded Cable Security Fleet and a trusted-spares stockpile for roughly $120–170M upfront.

themes.theme: Wartime repair capacity is the binding constraint

insights.claim: An adversary seeking to disrupt global communications only needs to damage submarine cables in multiple locations faster than the global repair system can restore them, making repair throughput rather than detection the key vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Cable resilience should be assessed on repair-queue capacity, not just route redundancy.
insights.quote: To effectively disrupt global communications, an adversary needs only to damage cables in multiple locations faster than the repair system can restore them.

insights.claim: Submarine cables suffer roughly 150 to 200 accidental faults per year, which are handled by only about 22 cable repair ships worldwide.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Tiny global repair fleet means simultaneous cuts could cascade into months-long outages.
insights.quote: Fishing gear, anchors, and other accidents damage submarine cables roughly 150 to 200 times annually, a number easily handled by the approximately 22 ships in the world equipped to repair subsea cables.

insights.claim: Clustered cable failures produce outsized outages: the 2022 Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai eruption isolated Tonga for five weeks with full restoration taking almost 18 months, and five Vietnamese international cables damaged in February 2023 took nine months to fully restore.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Multi-cut events stretch restoration from weeks to many months; price that tail risk for connectivity-dependent assets.

insights.claim: While the annual number of cable faults has stayed flat, the number and length of cables are growing, so the peacetime record of easy repair understates wartime risk from clustered failures, sabotage and conflict occurring together.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Peacetime reliability statistics are a misleading base rate for wartime connectivity planning.
insights.quote: A repair system sized for the rate of current accidents is not built to withstand an adversary that has learned to make attacks look like accidents.

insights.claim: An international cable repair takes about a month even in peacetime, so a handful of ships facing nine faults across two theaters (e.g., Taiwan plus the Red Sea) would need months to restore service.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: A two-theater cable campaign would mean prolonged Asia–Europe bandwidth constraints.

themes.theme: China dependency in Pacific cable repair

insights.claim: Pacific cable repairs under the Yokohama Zone maintenance agreement rely on three operators, including Shanghai-based S.B. Submarine Systems, majority owned by China Communications Services whose controlling shareholder is state-owned China Telecommunications Corporation; it has repaired cables owned by Google and Meta.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler Pacific cable resilience depends partly on Chinese state-linked repair capacity.

insights.claim: In a conflict over China or Taiwan, Beijing would not need to sabotage anything to cripple Pacific cable restoration; it could simply decline to send Chinese-controlled repair vessels.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: A Taiwan crisis would degrade Pacific connectivity via passive denial of repair, not just active cuts.
insights.quote: Beijing would not need to sabotage anything. It could simply decline to sail and repair.

insights.claim: Taiwan has 15 international cables landing at four stations; an end-2025 earthquake disrupted six of them with repairs lasting until May 2026, and the island sees seven to eight cable incidents a year, mostly from dragged anchors.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Taiwan's connectivity is concentrated and fragile; few vessels could replicate a six-cable outage deliberately.

insights.claim: Deliberately cutting six Taiwan cables near shore would require relatively few vessels, as shown by the single tanker Eagle S damaging five cables in the Gulf of Finland in December 2024, and Chinese vessels near Taiwan routinely switch off transponders.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Grey-zone cable sabotage is cheap and deniable; watch for anchor-drag incidents as escalation signals.
insights.locator: How large would a campaign need

insights.claim: In spring 2026 Britain, Norway and the U.S. tracked and disrupted a covert Russian Arctic exercise in which deep-sea submersibles simulated deploying a weapon to disable the two 1,400-km cables linking Svalbard, which hosts a satellite ground station serving Europe, the U.S. and Japan, to mainland Norway.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Russia is rehearsing cable attacks where repair is hardest; Arctic infrastructure carries elevated risk.

insights.claim: Russia's Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research operates at least eight nuclear-powered special-mission submarines plus surface ships like the Yantar carrying submersibles capable of 6,000-meter depths, and China has an advanced deep-sea cable cutting device.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Both major adversaries possess deep-water cable attack capability beyond anchor-drag deniability.
insights.locator: Adversaries are already building the means

insights.claim: Dense cable choke points such as Suez/Bab al-Mandeb, the Strait of Hormuz and the South China Sea offer easy environments for multiple hard-to-attribute cuts, which adversaries could also time to coincide with natural faults like underwater landslides.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Choke-point cable concentration is a systemic risk for Asia–Europe data flows.
insights.locator: Adversaries are already building the means

insights.claim: The planned 10,000-km Polar Connect cable from Sweden across the Arctic to Japan and North America, intended as a Red Sea alternative, would run close to Svalbard, in the same waters where Russia rehearsed disrupting cables.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Diversification routes can trade one geopolitical risk for another.

insights.claim: Low Earth orbit satellites are an access technology, not a backbone, and cannot replace cable capacity; their ground stations depend on cables and their signals can be jammed.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: LEO constellations are not a substitute hedge for cable outages at scale.
insights.quote: they remain an access technology, not a backbone, and cannot replace the capacity of the cables they would be backing up
insights.locator: A second objection is that low

insights.claim: The 2024 Red Sea incident in which Houthis struck the Rubymar, whose anchor dragged across three cables, affected an estimated quarter of Asia–Europe–Middle East traffic and took about six months to repair amid security concerns and a Yemeni permit dispute.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Conflict zones extend repair times and politicize permitting.
insights.locator: Repair and restoration in contested waters

themes.theme: Legal and insurance barriers to repair under fire

insights.claim: Cable repair ships have no immunity under the law of armed conflict, and because military traffic rides commercial cables, both cables and repair ships could be lawful targets; the 2025 Newport Manual treats military communications cables as military objectives.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Repair crews and owners face real targeting risk, deterring wartime service.

insights.claim: War-risk insurance can be canceled on as little as 72 hours' notice; after U.S. hostilities with Iran began on Feb. 28, 2026, insurers issued cancellation notices for Persian Gulf war cover within days, and by early March the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman and Persian Gulf were designated a Warlike Operations Area letting crews refuse to sail.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Insurance withdrawal is a fast-acting chokepoint on maritime services in conflict zones.
insights.quote: Insurance compounds the problem, because war coverage can be canceled on as little as 72 hours’ notice.

insights.claim: Naval escort may make a commercial repair ship a lawful military objective, so protection should be graduated: close escort for government-contracted ships (likely already military objectives) and distant area security for purely commercial ones.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Expect policy debate on convoy rules for civilian infrastructure ships.

themes.theme: Policy gaps and cost of a fix

insights.claim: The U.S. has no government-operated cable repair ship since the Navy's Zeus was deactivated in 2025; the Cable Security Fleet pays $10 million annually to retain two private ships that can be working far from their assigned ocean, such as the Dependable spending a month in the Indian Ocean in 2022.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: U.S. assured repair capacity is minimal; potential procurement opportunity for cable ship builders/operators.
insights.locator: The United States doesn’t have a government-operated

insights.claim: The Maritime Administration requested no funding for the Cable Security Fleet in fiscal year 2027, despite the authors' call to double it to four ships at about $20 million a year.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Watch FY2027 appropriations for cable-fleet funding signals.
insights.quote: Yet the Maritime Administration requested no funding for it in fiscal year 2027.
insights.locator: Third, fund the Cable Security Fleet

insights.claim: A new dedicated cable repair ship costs $52–100 million to build and $12–14 million a year to run; a new ship, doubled fleet and spares inventory together would cost roughly $120–170 million upfront and about $35 million a year, under half of the €347 million the EU committed this year to cable projects.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Modest-dollar program could become a budget line benefiting cable ship and spares suppliers.
insights.locator: Third, fund the Cable Security Fleet

insights.claim: Spare-parts supply chain is an underappreciated bottleneck: jointing kits, repeaters and matching cable are not interchangeable, most of Tonga's 18-month wait went to specifying and shipping replacement cable from France, and FCC Covered List rules in 2025 narrowed the supplier pool.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Trusted-spares stockpiling creates demand for non-Chinese cable component makers.
insights.quote: A repair ship is only as useful as the spares it carries

insights.claim: In 2026 the EU allocated €60 million (€20 million Baltics, €40 million Mediterranean and Atlantic) for modular cable repair equipment pre-positioned at ports that can be rapidly installed on pre-configured vessels; the U.S. has no equivalent.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Europe is ahead on cable resilience spending; a U.S. analog program is plausible.
insights.locator: Europe has begun addressing this problem.

insights.claim: The authors propose DHS designate submarine cables a critical infrastructure subsector, Congress create a federal restoration coordinator with emergency powers including Defense Production Act priority ratings for spares (requiring reauthorization beyond Dec. 11, 2026), and MARAD pre-arrange government-backed war-risk insurance.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: DPA reauthorization deadline Dec. 11, 2026 is a near-term policy catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: First, the Department of Homeland Security

insights.claim: New U.S. cable landings still require separate approvals from the Army Corps of Engineers, NOAA, state coastal agencies and local zoning boards despite the FCC's 2025 licensing streamlining, slowing route diversification.
insights.speaker: Anita Nikolich and Andrew Gallo
insights.so_what: Permitting friction limits new cable route buildout timelines.
